messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Call Center Agent
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Tran is a 60-year-old Vietnamese American woman who has worked for years as a call center agent, spending long shifts with a headset on in a crowded room of voices and scripted reassurance. She came to treatment after the sudden death of a loved one, a loss that still feels unfinished in her mind. When she speaks about it, the account catches and breaks apart. She can describe certain moments with painful precision and then, just as suddenly, the rest goes dark. There are flashes she cannot stop: a sound, a face, the sense of being pulled back into that day. But when she gets close to what happened just before the death was fully understood by the family, she finds herself mentally shutting the door, pushing the memory away before it can unfold. Over time, this jagged quality of remembering has made ordinary reminders feel dangerous. A funeral announcement, a cemetery passed from the car window, even the cry of a baby can strike her as if it belongs to the loss itself, because in her mind these fragments of memory arrive without warning and attach themselves to the present.

In the months after the death, Linh became frightened not only of grief but of her own reactions to it. When a memory fragment broke through, she could suddenly feel as if she were back inside the experience rather than remembering it from a distance. What frightened her most was how little control she had over it. She would be in her kitchen or sitting at her workstation and, for a few seconds, lose her sense of now; her body would tense, her chest would tighten, and she would be flooded with fear and sorrow so intense that she felt ashamed of it afterward. Nights became especially hard. She lay awake dreading what might surface if her mind went quiet, and the lack of sleep seemed to leave her even less able to keep the fragments contained. The more shaken and exhausted she felt, the less she could hold a full narrative in mind; the memory stayed broken into vivid pieces and blank spaces, returning in bursts rather than as something complete and past.

She responded the way many people do when something feels unbearable: she began arranging her life to avoid contact with it. She stopped going to funerals and refused to enter cemeteries. If relatives tried to mention the death, she redirected the conversation or left the room. She also withdrew from people she had once socialized with before the loss, in part because she knew they would remember the person who died and in part because she feared being seen while overcome. At work, where callers’ voices stream constantly through her headset, the sound of a baby in the background of a call can abruptly unsettle her; now she braces for it and sometimes asks to step away after certain calls, saying she needs water or a restroom break. This narrowing of her world has not brought relief. Because she keeps cutting off conversations and reminders, the memory has stayed unprocessed—still fragmented, still partly blocked—and ordinary grief-related events retain their power to startle her.

Her avoidance has also taught her to scan for danger in places she once moved through without thinking. She checks obituaries only accidentally and then quickly looks away, refuses invitations if she suspects there may be a memorial element, and keeps her distance from former family friends who might bring up the death. The vigilance is exhausting. She has come to believe that if she lets herself remember fully or speak openly, she will be swallowed by the same terror and grief that seize her in those flashback-like moments. That fear makes her avoid more, and because she avoids more, the memory remains chopped into isolated pieces that can be set off by the next funeral notice, the next cemetery, the next baby’s cry overheard through her headset. Even when she tries to understand what happened, she notices herself stopping just before the most painful part, as though her mind pulls away to protect her, only to leave her vulnerable to another sudden fragment later.

By the time she sought help, Linh was sleeping poorly, dreading both work and family gatherings, and feeling her marriage strained by her silence. Her husband knew she was suffering, but she had shared very little, convinced that talking would make everything worse. What finally brought her in was the sense that her life had become organized around not being reminded. She wants, cautiously, to be able to hear ordinary sounds, attend family rituals, and think about her loved one without feeling dragged back into the moment of loss. At the same time, she is deeply afraid that if she stops pushing the memory away, what comes back will be more than she can bear.
